spans.text: A distinctly Melanesian variety began to crystallize with the start of the Pacific labour trade in 1863, when Melanesians were recruited (and in some cases kidnapped) to become labourers on plantations in Queensland (Australia).

spans.text: In 1883 and 1884, some also came from the Bismarck Archipelago – islands to the north-east of mainland New Guinea, but many more from this region went to plantations in Samoa from 1879 to 1912.

entries.subject: New Guinea

spans.text: Contact with the Highlands of New Guinea did not occur until the 1930s, and the Tok Pisin currently spoken in this region displays a number of distinctive characteristics.

spans.text: Like many other contact languages, Tok Pisin has received its share of abuse and has been ridiculed as a corrupted or degraded form of English, especially by expatriates in the territory in earlier years, and some of these attitudes may still persist.
